b005: The website for a Greek literary quarterly. It should feel refined and a little literary, and the Greek needs to read as naturally as the English, since most of the archive is Greek.
b008: A deck introducing a new Vietnamese literary imprint to booksellers, presented in Vietnamese, and it should feel cultured.
b015: A news reader app for a Vietnamese daily, with all content in Vietnamese, that should feel precise and current.
b034: Slipcase and jacket for a boxed set of Russian classics. It has to feel authoritative and permanent, and the Cyrillic titling carries the whole design.
b038: A humour anthology, 320 pages set at 10.5pt on cream stock. The face needs a lively italic, which is used heavily for asides, ligatures that do not look prim, and enough character to carry a joke without becoming tiring across a full book. Old-style figures, and a display cut for the chapter openers from the same family.
b045: A deck presenting a Russian-language children's magazine to advertisers. Slides mix Cyrillic headlines at 44px with body copy at 18px, so we need at least four weights, properly drawn Cyrillic italics, and figures that read clearly in circulation charts. It should feel warm and family-oriented rather than corporate.
b070: Packaging for a boxed set of a Japanese manga imprint's English translations. The spine sets Japanese and Latin together, and it should feel playful without undercutting the artwork.
b080: A Vietnamese memoir, 280 pages printed at 11pt. Vietnamese stacks diacritics heavily, so the face needs marks that do not crowd the ascenders above them. We want old-style figures, a true italic, and a warm rather than neutral texture on the page.
b089: A mobile app for a serious daily newspaper that should feel credible.
b090: A Vietnamese war reportage collection, 240 pages at 10.5pt. The text should feel severe and unornamented, with strong vertical stress and tight spacing. Vietnamese diacritics have to stay unambiguous even in that setting, and we need a heavy display weight for the section titles.
b108: A print magazine about Tokyo street food, in Japanese and English, that should feel lively.
b125: The website of a regional independent newspaper. It should feel like part of the community rather than a wire service, and body text needs to stay comfortable for long articles read on a phone.
b136: A printed investigative journalism annual, published in Japanese and English. It has to carry gravity, and the Latin must not look flimsy beside the Japanese in the bilingual spreads.
b165: The jacket for a Greek poetry collection, with the title set in Greek, that should feel understated and beautiful.
b166: A Vietnamese online encyclopedia. Body at 16px, heavy internal cross-linking so links must be distinguishable without relying on colour alone, tabular figures for data tables, and Vietnamese diacritics that do not clip against the line box. We need a minimum of five weights and a monospace companion for code examples. Neutral and precise, no personality.
b167: A deck pitching a new design magazine to investors. It should look considered enough that the typography is itself part of the argument, and it will be shown both projected and as a PDF.
b168: A mobile app for an underground Japanese music magazine, with the interface in Japanese and English, that should feel abrasive.
b179: A deck for a Greek satirical website pitching to advertisers. Headlines run at 54px in Greek and body at 20px. We need Greek that is funny in its own forms rather than a neutral face carrying funny words, four weights, an italic, and figures that work in audience charts. It has to survive being projected badly.
b196: A Russian-language long-read app with a reading mode. It needs to feel precise and unobtrusive, and the Cyrillic must stay comfortable at the small sizes people actually use.
b200: A printed Greek food and travel quarterly, written in Greek and English, that should feel welcoming.
b205: A Russian collection of dissident essays, 200 pages at 10pt. The setting should feel stark and typewriter-adjacent without literally being a typewriter face. The Cyrillic must be drawn with the same severity as the Latin, we need a very heavy weight for the title pages, and the italic should read as emphasis rather than decoration.
b012: A pitch deck for a party game studio seeking funding. Slides run 40px headlines and 20px body, projected in bright rooms, so contrast matters. We need at least five weights, a display cut with real personality for the section breaks, and figures that stay readable in revenue projections. It should feel fun without looking amateur.
b017: A lore compendium for a violent Japanese action game, published in Japanese and English, and it should feel oppressive.
b020: A collector's art book for a Japanese role-playing game, 240 pages with Japanese and English side by side. The Latin has to pair with Noto Serif JP at matched weight and x-height, hold at 10pt across long captions, and offer old-style figures and true small caps. It prints on coated stock with fine hairlines, so nothing that breaks up at small sizes. Restrained and refined, not gothic.
b037: A mobile companion app for a Vietnamese esports league, with the interface in Vietnamese, that should feel sharp and technical.
b046: A deck for a Vietnamese game studio presenting engine performance results, in Vietnamese and English. It is dense with benchmark tables and needs figures that align, and it should read as rigorous rather than promotional.
b057: A Russian-language mod manager app that should feel utilitarian.
b066: The website for a Russian tactical shooter, in Russian and English. It carries a lot of weapon statistics in tables, so figures need to align, and the whole thing should feel engineered rather than styled.
b069: The site for a colourful indie puzzle game that should feel inviting.
b075: A printed strategy guide for a historical wargame set in ancient Greece, in Greek and English. Polytonic Greek is required for the period quotations. Body runs at 9.5pt in three columns with heavy unit-statistic tables, so tabular lining figures and a condensed cut are both necessary. It should read as scholarly and authoritative.
b081: Packaging for a family board game sold in Greece. The box carries rules text in Greek and English at small sizes, and it should feel welcoming to people who do not think of themselves as gamers.
b084: A printed rulebook for a Russian historical strategy game, set in Russian, that should feel weighty and official.
b095: A companion novel for a grim mythological action game, published in Greek and English. It is read in long sittings so it has to stay readable, but the page should still feel harsh.
b140: A narrative adventure game's in-world journal, published as a 180-page hardback. Text runs at 11pt with frequent italic passages standing in for handwriting, so the italic must be genuinely distinct rather than a slant. We need old-style figures, small caps for the in-world documents, and a face refined enough to feel like a period artefact without becoming pastiche.
b148: A deck presenting a cosy farming game to Japanese publishers, in Japanese and English. Headlines at 48px, body at 20px, projected. The Latin must pair with a rounded Japanese face without a weight clash, and we need four weights plus figures that read clearly in retention charts. It should feel gentle and inviting throughout.
b158: A Vietnamese-language visual novel published as a printed book, 300 pages at 11pt. Dialogue is heavily italicised, so the italic has to hold up across long passages. Vietnamese diacritics must not collide with descenders from the line above at the leading we can afford. The tone is affectionate and unhurried.
b159: Packaging for a collector's edition of a military simulation game. The box carries a lot of specification text in a fixed area, so a condensed cut is needed, plus tabular figures for the hardware requirements. Spot UV on the title means strokes cannot be too fine. It should read as serious and technical rather than flashy.
b181: A deck introducing a wholesome Russian mobile game to publishers, presented in Russian and English, that should feel friendly.
b195: The site for a Japanese puzzle game with a minimal aesthetic, in Japanese and English, and it should feel quiet and refined.
b199: The site for a Greek horror game. It is bilingual, and the Greek has to feel as menacing as the Latin, which rules out most of the obvious display faces.
b202: Packaging for a Vietnamese-developed survival horror game. Box text runs in Vietnamese and English at small sizes, and it needs to feel genuinely threatening while staying legible under shrinkwrap.
b210: A casual mobile game aimed at Greek players. The interface is dense with small Greek labels, and it should feel bright and inviting without the Greek becoming hard to parse.
